extracted.intended_audience: Researchers authoring or peer-reviewing in vivo animal experiments (authors, reviewers, journal editors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for how to report design, methods, animals, procedures, and statistical analyses of in vivo (animal) experiments to maximise transparency, reproducibility and validity of manuscripts. Targets the methods/results sections and supporting materials for animal studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary outcome measure specification
rubrics_metrics.description: If more than one outcome was assessed in hypothesis-testing studies using inferential statistics, explicitly identify the primary outcome measure and state whether it was defined prior to data collection and whether it was used in the sample size calculation. If there was no primary outcome measure, explicitly state so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A primary outcome defined in advance protects against selective outcome reporting (primary outcome switching) and p-hacking. Studies that claim hypothesis testing but do not specify a pre-defined primary outcome, or change it after data collection, risk selectively reporting only statistically significant results. Provide evidence (e.g. protocol registration) that the reported primary outcome reflects what was planned. Examples given include clear statements of primary and secondary endpoints and accompanying power calculations (see provided Example 1 and Example 2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Protocol registration
rubrics_metrics.description: Register a study protocol in advance to document planned primary outcomes and analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registering a protocol in advance protects against selective outcome reporting (data dredging, p-hacking) and provides evidence that the primary outcome reported in the manuscript accurately reflects what was planned. The guideline cross-references Item 19 (Protocol registration) for further detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical methods (Provide details for each analysis) — (7a)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide detailed description of the statistical methods used for each analysis, including software and version, so another researcher could re-analyse the raw data and obtain the same results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide analysis methods in advance. Report which method was used for which analysis and include: the outcome measures; the independent variables of interest; nuisance variables accounted for (blocking factors or covariates); what statistical analyses were performed and references for methods used; how missing values were handled; adjustment for multiple comparisons; and the software package and version used (include computer code if available). Describe the experimental hierarchy and clustering (cage, litter, animal effects) and how these were handled (include as random effects, blocking, or aggregate appropriately). For bespoke analyses (e.g. complex regression), describe the analysis pipeline including starting model and any model simplification steps. When reporting descriptive statistics, explicitly state which measure of central tendency (mean/median) and which measure of variability (SD/range/IQR) are reported, and describe any modifications made to raw data before analysis (e.g. normalization against a housekeeping gene). Refer to SAMPL guidelines for further statistical reporting guidance. Examples in the text show typical reporting of model, blocking factors, transformations, and significance thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of statistical assumptions and corrective actions — (7b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe methods used to assess whether the data met the assumptions of the statistical approach, and report what was done if assumptions were not met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State for each statistical test the type of outcome measure and the methods used to test assumptions. For parametric tests (t-test, ANOVA, etc.) describe checks for continuity, normality of residuals, independence, and homogeneity of variances. Mention which tests were used (e.g. Shapiro–Wilk, Kolmogorov–Smirnov), but note their limitations (sensitivity to sample size); consider visual diagnostics (normal probability plots, residual vs fitted plots, boxplots). If assumptions fail, report transformations applied (specify exact transform and which outcomes it was applied to) or alternative analyses used (e.g. non-parametric tests). If assumptions were not tested, state this explicitly. Examples demonstrate reporting of normality/homoscedasticity testing and transforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about all analyses performed (avoid p-hacking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Report all analyses performed in full, including exploratory and hypothesis-testing analyses, to avoid selective reporting of only statistically significant results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysing data using different methods and selectively reporting those with statistically significant results constitutes p-hacking and introduces bias. Provide complete reporting of all analyses, clearly labelling exploratory vs pre-specified hypothesis-testing analyses. Where multiple outcomes or comparisons exist, report adjustments for multiple comparisons and full analysis outputs or code where feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental animals — species-appropriate details (8a)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide species-appropriate details of animals used, including species, strain and substrain, sex, age or developmental stage, and, if relevant, weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These characteristics influence experimental results and are critical for internal and external validity and reproducibility. Report summary statistics for each experimental group (e.g. mean ± SD) and baseline values for individuals if possible (supplementary data or repository). Indicate when weight/age were measured. For many species, precise age is more informative than vague developmental descriptors; however, report developmental stage where more appropriate. If reporting sex or weight is not feasible, provide a justification. Examples show explicit reporting of strains, ages, weights, and developmental stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animal provenance, health, and genetic modification status (8b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide details on animals' provenance, health/immune status, genetic modification status and genotype, and any previous procedures they underwent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different suppliers, colony histories, health/pathogen status, or prior procedures can affect physiology and outcomes—report these details (e.g. SPF status and list of pathogens tested). For genetically modified animals, describe modification type (knockout/overexpression), genotype (homozygous/heterozygous), targeted genes, methods used to generate animals, how modification was confirmed, and details of control animals (e.g. littermates). Use correct nomenclature and RRIDs where applicable; guideline lists authoritative nomenclature resources for mice, rats, zebrafish, Xenopus, Drosophila, C. elegans. Examples include detailed constructs, supplier information, and breeding/backcross histories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental procedures — what, how, and what was used (9a)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each experimental group (including controls), describe the procedures in enough detail for replication: what was done, how it was done, and what was used (reagents, equipment, protocols).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include procedures used to develop models (e.g. induction of pathology), outcome measurement methods, and pre-/post-experimental procedures (handling, welfare monitoring, euthanasia). Provide details specific to intervention types: pharmacological (formulation, dose, volume, route, frequency, vehicle, evidence of tissue targeting), surgical (procedure description, anaesthetic including dose, analgesia, aseptic technique, monitoring), pathogen infection (agent, dose, route, timing), euthanasia (method, humane standards, timing, tissues collected). Report cell line identification, provenance, authentication, RRIDs. For reagents and equipment give manufacturer, supplier, catalogue and lot numbers where applicable, and RRIDs. Where available, cite or provide protocol DOIs (e.g. protocols.io). Examples include step-by-step surgical/anesthetic regimens, diet interventions with protocol links, and molecular assay reagent details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and frequency of procedures and measurements (9b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly report when and how often experimental procedures and measurements were performed, including light/dark cycle and circadian timing where relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report frequency and timing of measurements (e.g. every 5 minutes, baseline and post-injury timepoints), light/dark cycle (e.g. 12L:12D), lights-on time, intervals between procedures and measurements, and timing/frequency of welfare assessments. If timing varies between animals, provide per-animal timing as supplementary material. Examples show minute-by-minute monitoring schedules and multi-day clamp procedures with recovery intervals. Consider circadian effects and species activity patterns when scheduling and reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Location and acclimatisation periods (9c)
rubrics_metrics.description: Report where experiments were conducted and details of any acclimatisation periods (e.g. after transport) before the experiment began.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physiological acclimatisation after stressful events (transport, transfer between facilities) allows stabilization of responses and varies by species and outcome; report duration and conditions of acclimatisation (often 24 hours to >1 week depending on species). Include location details (facility/room) when relevant to environmental effects. This information helps assess whether animals were physiologically stable at experiment start.
